chunks: And as for what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Abu al-Hassan (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him: 'I have a female slave who has no place with me (i.e., I do not desire her), and she is worth the price, except that I had sworn an oath regarding her, saying: 'It is upon me to God that I will never sell her.' And I have a need for her price to reduce expenses.' He said: 'It is for you according to your word.' We mentioned this report in the Chapter on Categories of Oaths in the narration of al-Saffar because he narrated it with the wording of 'oath' (yamin), and we repeated it here because it contains the wording of 'vow' (nadhru). The meaning within it is the meaning we mentioned: that it is to be understood either as recommended (istihbab) or as removing suitability in selling her both religiously and mundanely, and the two matters stand on equal footing, as we said there.
ai.seo_question: How to interpret a vow of 'never selling' a slave or property when financial need arises?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that a vow of perpetual retention is not absolute, permitting the sale of the slave to alleviate financial burden, as the underlying meaning balances religious and worldly benefits. This narration is cross-referenced with the chapter on oaths, noting that while the text uses the term 'vow' (nadr), its legal ruling aligns with the interpretation of oaths (yamin) discussed in the transmission of al-Saffar, emphasizing that the vow carries a recommended rather than strictly prohibitive weight.
